# Latency and Congestion

**Playback latency** is the time between capturing media and presenting it to a viewer. Some of that time is spent processing and moving data; some is spent waiting in queues. A connection can keep delivering objects while the viewer falls seconds behind.

We’ll work out where the delay comes from, then follow a queue as it grows. That leads to the choices a sender can make: send less, favor some content, or stop sending old content. Finally, we’ll look at how the player catches up. The numbers are made up to keep the examples easy to calculate.

## Which rates and delays are we measuring? {#units-before-arithmetic}

A **bit** is a binary digit; a **byte** contains eight bits. Network rates commonly use bits per second, while file sizes commonly use bytes. Here, the prefixes are decimal: one megabit is one million bits.

| Measure | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Bitrate, in Mb/s | Bits produced or carried each second | 4 Mb/s of encoded media |
| Byte rate, in MB/s | Bytes produced or carried each second | 4 Mb/s = 0.5 MB/s, before transport overhead |
| Available capacity | The rate a path can currently sustain for this traffic | A 2 Mb/s path cannot keep up with a 4 Mb/s source |
| Throughput | The transfer rate actually achieved | Measure delivered bytes over a stated interval |
| RTT, in milliseconds | Network round-trip time | A 40 ms RTT is not a 40 ms playback delay |
| Playback latency | Delay from capture to presentation | Includes processing and buffering as well as transit |

A connection might carry plenty of video each second while taking a long time to deliver any one frame. That’s why we measure both capacity and delay. When comparing network capacity with media bitrate, leave room for packet headers and other transport overhead too.

## Where does playback delay come from? {#where-the-time-goes}

Capture-to-display latency includes capture, encoding, network transit, buffering, decoding, and presentation. A relay or operating system can add another queue along the way. Measuring only the network leaves much of the path unexplained.

Suppose one frame spends its time like this:

| Stage | Time |
| --- | ---: |
| Capture | 20 ms |
| Encode | 35 ms |
| Network | 45 ms |
| Playback buffer | 80 ms |
| Decode and display | 20 ms |
| Total | 200 ms |

We could save five milliseconds on the network and bring the total down to 195 ms. The 80 ms playback buffer looks like a bigger opportunity. But if we shrink it, frames that arrive a little late are more likely to miss their playback time. That’s the tradeoff we’re making.

For a student just listening, a slightly longer wait might be fine if it prevents interruptions. For a student asking a question, that same wait makes the conversation awkward. They may prefer a few skipped pictures so they can keep talking.

## Why does the queue keep growing? {#how-a-queue-grows}

Suppose the publisher produces four megabits each second while Alice's path carries two. Each second adds two megabits to a queue. After five seconds, ten megabits are waiting, ignoring overhead. Even if production stops at that moment, sending that backlog at two megabits per second takes another five seconds.

As long as the publisher keeps producing four megabits per second, the queue keeps growing. To catch up, it needs to produce less data, or the system needs to drop some of the data already waiting.

**Congestion control** limits what the transport sends to avoid overwhelming the network. The transport adjusts its sending rate in response to congestion signals; it does not directly know the path’s available capacity. That protects the path, but it cannot decide whether Alice would prefer a smaller picture or an old high-resolution one. That is the job of **media adaptation**. See [RFC 9002 §7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9002.html#section-7).

One option is for Alice’s player to ask for a lower-bitrate rendition. Another is for the publisher to lower its encoding bitrate. Once less data enters the queue than leaves it, the backlog can shrink. If that would take too long, the system can also skip old content to get Alice back near live.

### Congestion control, flow control, and adaptation

The transport and application each have a part to play:

| Mechanism | Question it answers | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| QUIC congestion control | How much traffic can this network path carry? | Packet loss causes the sender to reduce its sending rate |
| QUIC flow control | How much stream data is the receiver willing to accept? | The receiver stops granting more credit while its buffers are full |
| Media adaptation | How much media should the application produce or request? | The player switches from a 4 Mb/s rendition to a 1 Mb/s rendition |

Flow control protects the receiver with limits on individual streams and the connection as a whole. It does not measure whether a frame is still worth displaying. See [RFC 9000 §4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html#section-4). A player can therefore receive data reliably and within its allowed limits while still falling behind the lecture.

## How do priorities choose what to send? {#choosing-which-content-to-send}

Suppose Alice’s connection can no longer keep up with both audio and video. Sending audio first may let her keep following the lecture while the picture struggles. The **scheduler** chooses which pending data to send, so it needs to know that audio matters more here.

MOQT expresses these choices through priorities and group ordering. In draft-21, smaller priority numbers mean more urgent work. Its recommended scheduler checks subscriber priority first, then publisher priority. When priorities are equal within a subscription, group ordering helps decide which group goes first. Implementations can use other scheduling algorithms. See [§5.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-5.1) for the full recommendation.

If we send audio first and it uses all the available capacity, video still has to wait. Priority helps us choose who waits; a timeout lets us decide when waiting has gone on too long. When using a library, check its priority conventions, since moq-lite and MOQT use different rules.

## When should delivery stop? {#abandoning-old-content-safely}

Suppose video group 41 remains incomplete while group 42 provides a fresh decoding starting point. Finishing group 41 would preserve older pictures, but sending group 42 may bring Alice closer to the lecturer. Independent groups make that choice possible without requiring every preceding picture.

The sender still has to respect the stream's structure. A reliable byte stream cannot deliver later bytes past a missing section. To abandon a subgroup's remaining stream data, MOQT resets that stream. A receiver must then use the media format's dependencies to decide where decoding can resume.

Draft-21 has two optional timeouts for this. One checks how long an object has waited before entering the transport. The other limits the time to finish delivering a completed subgroup. We’ll look at each separately, using a relay’s clock and a 100 ms limit. See [§5.2](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-moq-transport-21#section-5.2).

### Waiting to enter the transport

The **object delivery timeout** measures age from when the last byte of an object's header arrives from upstream. At the original publisher, it starts when the application supplies that header. Before handing the object to the underlying transport, the implementation checks its age.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    accTitle: Object delivery timeout example
    accDescr: The relay receives the complete object header at zero milliseconds. At 120 milliseconds it checks whether to send the object. The 100 millisecond limit has passed, so it resets a subgroup stream or drops a datagram.
    A["0 ms: header received"] --> B["120 ms: ready to send"]
    B --> C["Age exceeds 100 ms"]
    C --> D["Subgroup: reset stream"]
    C --> E["Datagram: drop it"]
```

Here the object has already spent too long waiting before transmission. For a subgroup, expiry resets the stream rather than removing a few bytes from its middle. For a datagram, the expired message is dropped.

This check is most effective when the application can still control the queue. If it hands large amounts of data to the transport in advance, expired bytes may already be beyond its reach. Draft-21 therefore recommends minimizing transport buffering and checking expiry before retransmission where the transport interface permits it.

### Waiting for delivery to finish

The **subgroup delivery timeout** starts when the endpoint knows all objects in the subgroup have been published. At a relay, receiving the upstream stream's `FIN` provides that information. This timer covers remaining delivery work, including recovery after packet loss.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    accTitle: Subgroup delivery timeout example
    accDescr: At 50 milliseconds the relay learns the subgroup is complete and starts a 100 millisecond timer. At 150 milliseconds it resets the stream if transport delivery is still incomplete.
    A["50 ms: subgroup complete"] --> B["Start 100 ms timer"]
    B --> C["150 ms: still undelivered?"]
    C -->|Yes| D["Reset stream"]
    C -->|No| E["Delivery finished"]
```

The transport must reach what the specification calls “all data committed” before the timer expires: its completion state for delivering the data, beyond merely accepting bytes into a send buffer. This concerns transport delivery, not whether the player has decoded or displayed the media. Otherwise, the stream is reset. Unlike the object age check, this timer can expire after the sender has handed all the data to the transport.

For datagrams, the subgroup timeout instead uses the same age check as the object timeout; if both are nonzero, the smaller value applies. Zero disables the corresponding timeout. These rules describe a single hop's delivery decisions. They do not create a capture-to-display deadline across the whole relay network.

### Is moq-lite's maximum age the same timer?

No. The moq.dev [moq-lite guide](https://doc.moq.dev/concept/moq-lite) describes a maximum age relative to the media timeline. Older groups can become unwanted as newer media appears. A network stall by itself does not advance that timeline, and sending a backlog in a burst does not make its media new.

Both publisher and subscriber apply the limit. This matters when viewers share upstream delivery: content still useful to a patient viewer may already be too old for someone speaking in the call. Keep this implementation setting separate from draft-21's local delivery timers and from a player's capture-to-display delay.

## How does the player return to live? {#returning-to-live-playback}

After the network recovers, Alice may still be watching frames that reached her earlier. A fresh transport queue does not empty the player's playback queue. The player needs its own policy for skipping stale decoded frames or moving its presentation clock forward, while respecting audio synchronization and decoding dependencies.

This gives us two places to observe recovery: when fresh objects arrive, and when fresh content is actually displayed. Measuring both distinguishes network backlog from playback backlog.

A useful experiment briefly reduces available bandwidth and then restores it. Watch whether playback returns near live, stays behind, or repeatedly changes rendition. Record interruptions as well as average delay. A large keyframe can briefly exceed the path's capacity even when the average bitrate fits, so the sequence of events matters.

Use a repeatable recorded source for the first experiment. It keeps scene complexity and encoder load stable while you investigate the network response. Once you understand that run, repeat on real devices and networks, where capture, rendering, and additional queues can change the result.
